params.question: The principal blood supply to the lower pole of the palatine tonsil is the tonsillar branch of which artery?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The maxillary artery supplies deep structures of the face and the meningeal region, not the palatine tonsil directly. The tonsillar branch of the facial artery is the key vessel at the lower pole.

The lingual artery may contribute minor branches to the tonsillar region, but the principal supply to the lower pole is the tonsillar branch of the facial artery — the vessel that must be secured during tonsillectomy.
Correct. The tonsillar branch of the facial artery enters at the lower pole and is the main vessel that must be secured during tonsillectomy dissection to achieve haemostasis.
The ascending pharyngeal artery contributes to the pharyngeal blood supply but is not the principal vessel at the lower pole. The tonsillar branch of the facial artery is the key surgical vessel.

overallFeedback.feedback: The principal blood supply to the lower pole of the palatine tonsil is the tonsillar branch of the facial artery. Securing this vessel is essential for haemostasis during tonsillectomy.
The tonsillar branch of the facial artery at the lower pole is the most important vessel to secure during tonsillectomy — a critical landmark in the peritonsillar dissection plane.

params.question: A medical student prescribes amoxicillin for a patient with tonsillitis who is later found to have Epstein-Barr virus infection. What is the most likely adverse consequence?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While EBV can itself cause mild hepatitis, the specific adverse consequence of giving amoxicillin to an EBV-infected patient is a widespread maculopapular rash occurring in 80–100% of cases.

answers.text: A widespread maculopapular rash in the majority of patients

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Amoxicillin triggers a florid maculopapular rash in 80–100% of patients with infectious mononucleosis. Always check for posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly before prescribing any aminopenicillin for tonsillitis.
Anaphylaxis is a risk of true penicillin allergy in any patient and is not specific to EBV. The EBV-specific reaction to amoxicillin is a florid maculopapular rash in 80–100% of infected patients.

answers.text: Antibiotic resistance rendering future streptococcal treatment ineffective

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Antibiotic resistance is a general concern with inappropriate prescribing but is not the specific consequence here. Amoxicillin in EBV causes a florid maculopapular rash in 80–100% of infected patients.

overallFeedback.feedback: Amoxicillin causes a florid maculopapular rash in 80–100% of patients with EBV infection. Before prescribing any aminopenicillin for tonsillitis, always exclude infectious mononucleosis by checking for posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly.

This prescribing trap is a key safety rule: never give amoxicillin without first ruling out EBV. Check for splenomegaly and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy — both point strongly to infectious mononucleosis.

params.question: A 6-year-old child has documented records showing five episodes of sore throat per year for two consecutive years. Each episode had fever above 38.3°C and cervical lymphadenopathy, but throat cultures were not performed. Does this child satisfy the Paradise criteria for tonsillectomy?

answers.text: No, because throat cultures must be positive for Group A streptococcus in every episode

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A positive GAS culture is only one of four acceptable objective features. Fever above 38.3°C, cervical lymphadenopathy, or tonsillar exudate each independently satisfies the objective criterion — cultures are not mandatory.

answers.text: No, because a minimum of seven episodes in a single year is always required

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Seven episodes in one year is only one of three qualifying thresholds. The criteria also accept 5 per year for 2 consecutive years or 3 per year for 3 years — this child meets the second threshold.

answers.text: No, because the criteria require three episodes per year for at least three consecutive years as the minimum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Three per year for three years is one qualifying threshold, but it is not the only one. Five per year for two consecutive years also qualifies, and this child meets that threshold with documented objective features.

answers.text: Yes, because five episodes per year for two consecutive years with documented objective features meets the threshold

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Paradise criteria accept three frequency thresholds: 7 in 1 year, 5 per year for 2 years, or 3 per year for 3 years. Each episode needs at least one objective feature — fever, lymphadenopathy, exudate, or positive culture. This child meets the 5-per-year-for-2-years threshold with documented fever and lymphadenopathy.

overallFeedback.feedback: The Paradise criteria accept three frequency thresholds: 7 in 1 year, 5 per year for 2 consecutive years, or 3 per year for 3 years. Each episode must include a sore throat plus at least one objective feature (fever >38.3°C, cervical lymphadenopathy, exudate, or positive GAS swab). Documented records are required — parental recall alone does not suffice.
The Paradise criteria require documented episodes — not parental recall alone — each with at least one objective feature. This child clearly meets the 5-per-year-for-2-years threshold.

interactions.label: A child presents with fresh bleeding from the tonsillar fossa on day seven after

params.question: A child presents with fresh bleeding from the tonsillar fossa on day seven after tonsillectomy. Which type of post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage is this, and what is its mechanism?

answers.text: Reactionary haemorrhage — from rising blood pressure as anaesthetic vasoconstriction reverses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Reactionary haemorrhage occurs within the first 24 hours as blood pressure rises post-anaesthesia. Bleeding on day 7 falls squarely in the secondary haemorrhage window (day 5–10).

answers.text: Primary haemorrhage — from a vessel inadequately secured during the operation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Primary haemorrhage occurs within the first 24 hours, typically from an unsecured surgical vessel. Day 7 bleeding is secondary haemorrhage from sloughing of the healing eschar.

answers.text: Secondary haemorrhage — from re-infection of the tonsillar fossa causing tissue necrosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While infection can contribute to premature eschar breakdown, the direct mechanism of secondary haemorrhage is sloughing of the fibrinous eschar (the white healing crust) that exposes underlying vessels — not a fresh bacterial infection.

answers.text: Secondary haemorrhage — from sloughing of the fibrinous eschar exposing underlying vessels

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Secondary haemorrhage occurs between day 5 and day 10 when the fibrinous eschar sloughs from the tonsillar fossa, exposing underlying vessels. It is the most dangerous type because it strikes when the patient is at home and vigilance is lowest.

overallFeedback.feedback: Bleeding on day 7 is secondary haemorrhage — caused by sloughing of the fibrinous eschar that protected the tonsillar fossa during healing. It occurs between day 5 and day 10, precisely when the patient is at home and vigilance is lowest. Any post-tonsillectomy oral bleeding demands immediate Emergency Department evaluation.

Secondary haemorrhage (day 5–10) is the most dangerous post-tonsillectomy complication. Every family must be warned: any blood from the mouth in the two weeks after surgery means an immediate Emergency Department visit, no exceptions.
